terms.gloss: popular, well liked, in favour (of a person)
terms.grammar: adjective; popular with someone, grātiōsus apud aliquem
evidence: Cic. Off. 3.58: apud omnēs ōrdinēs grātiōsus (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 156, 363: popular, grātiōsus; to be popular with someone, grātiōsus esse apud aliquem
terms.comment: A favourite word of Cicero’s, used mostly of persons (Lewis & Short). Popularity is grātia (Traupman 156).

evidence: Cic. Lig. 37: nihil est tam populāre quam bonitās
Cic. Agr. 2.9: quid enim est tam populāre quam pāx?
terms.comment: Of things and measures that please the public. Of a politician, populāris is one who courts the crowd: Cicero glosses it assentātor, a flatterer (Lael. 95). As a noun it is a fellow countryman.

evidence: Caes. BG 1.3: maximē plēbī acceptus erat

terms.comment: Not before Augustus; perhaps first in Vell. 2.34 (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: of a place: much frequented, busy, popular
evidence: Cic. Imp. Pomp. 33: portus celeberrimus (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Verr. 2.3.133: in forō celeberrimō (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: commonly, generally (as most people say or think)
terms.comment: For “popular” in the sense “of people in general”: a popular belief is one held by most people, vulgō.

phrases.latin: nihil est tam populāre quam bonitās
phrases.english: nothing is so popular as kindness

phrases.latin: quantō plūs propinquōrum, quantō major adfīnium numerus, tantō grātiōsior senectūs
phrases.english: the more kinsfolk and the greater the number of in-laws, the more cherished is old age
